design_detail: Combined review in three parts (Drug and Alcohol Dependence 2018; read as the NIH author manuscript). (1) A prevalence meta-analysis of 16 estimates of alcohol and cannabis use among people who use cocaine: 11 from one PubMed search (humans, January 1990 to June 2017) and 5 from the authors' own secondary analyses of US datasets (the 2014 NSDUH and four community, outreach and drug-court studies in St Louis and north central Florida), pooled with random-effects models into four estimates (simultaneous or concurrent use; alcohol or cannabis). (2) A narrative review, without a stated search, of human and animal studies on combining cocaine with alcohol or cannabis (effects, metabolism, brain imaging, cognition, treatment outcome). (3) An exploratory count of how often the 40 most recent human cocaine neuroimaging studies and 40 recent animal cocaine studies excluded or modelled alcohol and cannabis. The card's design is meta-analysis because the pooled prevalences are the paper's quantitative result; the narrative part is described here but its cited studies are not appraised.
can_establish: That in every sample the review found, a large share of people who use cocaine also used alcohol, and in most samples cannabis, in the same period or on the same occasions, and that recent human cocaine imaging studies seldom excluded people who drink or use cannabis while recent animal cocaine studies almost never gave a second drug.
cannot_establish: A single meaningful prevalence of co-use for any defined population (source estimates run from about a quarter to nearly all people who use cocaine depending on sample and definition, I² 97–99%), whether alcohol co-use is more common than cannabis co-use (not tested), or any effect of combining drugs on the brain, behaviour or treatment (the narrative part is unsystematic and rests mostly on single small studies, unappraised).

sample.recruitment: Prevalence sources: one PubMed search (cocaine AND co-administration, concomitant, simultaneous or concurrent; humans; January 1990 to June 2017) gave 770 records, 134 full texts and 11 included studies; the authors added five datasets they analysed themselves: the 2014 NSDUH (US national), Women Teaching Women (St Louis community outreach, 2000–2006), Sisters Teaching Options for Prevention (St Louis drug courts, 2005–2008), the Prescription Drug Misuse, Abuse, and Dependence study (St Louis outreach, 2008–2010) and HealthStreet (north central Florida community engagement, 2011–2017) (Methods › 2.1, 2nd–4th paragraphs; Table 1). Neuroimaging count: the 40 most recent PubMed records for fMRI AND cocaine as of 1 January 2018 with cocaine use as the independent variable; animal count: recent PubMed records for cocaine filtered to other animals, in vivo cocaine administration in mammals (2.3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Given only as reasons for exclusion at full text (134): 54 without the combinations of interest, 24 small clinical samples judged unable to estimate general-population prevalence, 17 not relevant to prevalence, 18 not retrievable or case reports, post-mortem or neurological studies, 6 reviews, 3 without combination-specific prevalence, 1 not in English. Four clinical samples were said to be kept because they were large, multi-site or emergency-department based (2.1, 3rd paragraph). Where a source gave several time windows the shortest was used; where it gave powder and crack cocaine separately the powder figure was used (2.1, 5th paragraph).
sample.demographics: Table 1: 10 US, 3 Canadian, 2 Brazilian and 1 Danish source, study periods 1985 to 2017. Literature sources had 98 to 36,425 participants (the authors' 2014 NSDUH analysis 55,271); cocaine-using subsamples ranged from 17 (rave attendees) to 1,183 (treatment-seeking people with cocaine dependence). Women 0% (Brazilian recreational bodybuilders) to 100% (two St Louis samples); mean ages 22 to 44 (3.1.1, 1st paragraph). Samples: national household surveys, community outreach, drug courts, college students, rave attendees, bodybuilders, people who use MDMA or hallucinogens, people who use prescription drugs non-medically, people in treatment, emergency-department patients.
sample.selection_effects: One database and one search string, English only (one study excluded for language), no grey literature, reference-list or citation searching. Five of the 16 estimates come from the authors' own analyses, four of them from one research programme (L.B. Cottler's) in St Louis and Florida, two of these women-only and one from drug courts. The populations range from household surveys to treatment services and emergency departments, so the pooled figures average across groups whose co-use differs by design. Tobacco and nicotine were not considered (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Co-use as each source defined it: self-report in structured interviews or surveys in 15 sources; urine results from emergency-department records in one (Vanek et al., 1996). Simultaneous use meant use at the same time or within a couple of hours, co-administration during a session, co-use at first cocaine use, using alcohol or cannabis to come down from a cocaine high (WTW, STOP), or using them together with cocaine and a prescription drug in the past 12 months (Rx); concurrent use meant both substances within 30 days, 6 months, a year, a lifetime, both positive in a urine test, or an unstated window (Schwingel et al., 2014) (3.1.1, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, Measure column). The review's own definitions: same occasion with overlapping consumption or effects (simultaneous); within a specified period (concurrent) (2.1, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not part of the prevalence estimates; amounts and frequency of co-use were not extracted. Powder and crack cocaine are mixed across sources (powder preferred where both were reported).
exposure.polysubstance: The subject of the review. Only cocaine with alcohol and cocaine with cannabis were pooled; tobacco was not recorded in most sources, which the authors name as a gap (Discussion, 4th paragraph); cocaine with heroin was left to an earlier review (2.2).

comparison.controls: None for the prevalence estimates (single-group proportions). The exploratory count compares recent human with recent animal cocaine studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the prevalence estimates. The imaging studies summarized in the narrative part are cross-sectional, without measures from before use.

outcomes.instruments: Proportion of people who use cocaine reporting, or testing positive for, alcohol or cannabis use, from each source's own instrument: NSDUH computer-assisted interviews; the Substance Abuse Module (the authors' St Louis studies); the Customary Drinking and Drug use Record; a health intake form; structured face-to-face interviews; medical-record urine results (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not assessed: no study-level appraisal of sampling, measurement or response.
outcomes.operationalization: Co-use prevalence per source at the shortest reported window, among people who use cocaine as each source defined them (past-30-day, lifetime or new use, treatment-seeking people with dependence, emergency-department patients).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (four descriptive pooled proportions; the human–animal comparison used two Fisher's exact tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. One author ran the epidemiological search and the meta-analysis (Author information › Contributors).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooled prevalence among people who use cocaine: simultaneous alcohol use 74% (95% CI 50–89%), simultaneous cannabis use 38% (20–60%), concurrent alcohol use 77% (62–87%), concurrent cannabis use 64% (47–79%) (3.1.2, 2nd paragraph). I² 97% to 99% in all four analyses, chi-square p<0.01 (3.1.2, 1st paragraph). The number of sources in each pooled estimate, the per-source weights and the per-analysis I² appear only in Figure 1 (forest plots), an image that was not viewable in this reading (figure image not viewable). Ranges across sources as stated in the text: simultaneous alcohol 24–98%, simultaneous cannabis 12–76%, concurrent alcohol 37–96%, concurrent cannabis 43–94% (3.1.1, 1st paragraph; three of these do not match Table 1, see reporting issues). Human vs animal cocaine studies that included co-use: alcohol 75% vs 5%, cannabis 72.5% vs 0% of 40 studies each, Fisher's exact p<0.0001 (3.3). An editors' recalculation from Table 1 reproduces two of the four pooled values, not the other two (see reporting issues).
analysis.covariates: None. No subgroup analysis or meta-regression by population, definition, time window, country or period.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: No prediction intervals or tau², and no assessment of small-study effects. The choice between fixed and random effects was made by a test for heterogeneity (2.1, 5th paragraph). The scale on which proportions were pooled is not stated.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 16 heterogeneous sources, alcohol use alongside cocaine was common in every sample and cannabis use in most; the pooled random-effects averages (74% and 77% for alcohol, 38% and 64% for cannabis) carry wide intervals and I² of 97–99%, and the lowest source values come from the narrowest definition (using alcohol or cannabis to come down from a cocaine high). The narrative part rests on single small laboratory studies, one research group's cross-sectional imaging series and monkey studies with mixed results.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract gives the four pooled prevalences without their intervals or the heterogeneity, as if each were the prevalence among people who use cocaine. The results text calls the findings consistent with the hypothesis that alcohol co-use is more common than cannabis co-use (3.1.2, 2nd paragraph), though no comparison was tested and the intervals overlap. The narrative concludes that concurrent cocaine and alcohol dependence "causes greater structural defects in white-matter" (3.2.3, 1st paragraph) from cross-sectional group comparisons, and that simultaneous cocaine and alcohol increases the reinforcing qualities of dopamine agonists (3.2.1, 3rd paragraph), a generalization from a handful of monkeys in studies with mixed results (no change in cocaine intake on average after alcohol pretreatment, with increases in 2 of 4 monkeys and in nomifensine self-administration; less cocaine taken after the highest alcohol dose) and from one study phase in which 5 of 6 monkeys came to take previously non-reinforcing cocaine doses while alcohol was available daily from 4 hours after the cocaine sessions, that is, not at the same time. The human–animal comparison counts a human study as including co-use when it did not exclude people who drink or use cannabis, but an animal study only when it gave a second drug, so the two percentages measure different things. The discussion does acknowledge the heterogeneity of samples and definitions (Discussion, 1st paragraph).

timeline.event: Grant and Harford (1990), 1985 US household survey: the only included source that reported both simultaneous and concurrent cocaine–alcohol use (as described in this review).
Human laboratory study of cocaine and alcohol given together (McCance-Katz et al., 1998), cited here for higher plasma cocaine and cocaethylene formation
Overview of polydrug use as a confounder in studies of people who use MDMA (Gouzoulis-Mayfrank & Daumann, 2006): the same design problem for another drug
Review of polysubstance use: diagnostic challenges, patterns of use and health (Connor et al., 2014)

replication.where_it_stands: That most people who use cocaine also drink alcohol, and many use cannabis, holds in every sample listed here; a defensible single figure would need a systematic, appraised synthesis stratified by population and definition, which this review does not provide. Reviews of latent classes of polysubstance use (Tomczyk et al., 2016; LeComte et al., 2025; on the General list, not yet appraised) describe patterns of use in a different way.

Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Population-representative surveys in several countries that ask people who use cocaine about co-use with one shared definition of same-occasion and same-period use (ideally with event-level diaries), and a registered systematic review that searches several databases, screens and extracts in duplicate, appraises each source and reports estimates stratified by population and definition, with prediction intervals.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Several critical weaknesses: no protocol, one database, no list of exclusions, no appraisal of the sources, pooling of incompatible definitions and populations with I² of 97–99% without investigating why, and no consideration of bias in interpreting the results. The review may be cited for the observation that every sample it found showed high co-use of alcohol, and in most cases cannabis, among people who use cocaine, together with the range across samples and definitions, and for its count of recent human and animal cocaine studies that did or did not handle co-use. It should not be cited for a single prevalence figure without the interval, the heterogeneity and the range. The narrative section is a pointer to primary studies, not evidence for effects of combining drugs.

key_findings.finding: Pooled random-effects prevalence among people who use cocaine: simultaneous alcohol use 74% (95% CI 50–89%), simultaneous cannabis use 38% (20–60%), concurrent alcohol use 77% (62–87%), concurrent cannabis use 64% (47–79%).
key_findings.locator: 3. Results › 3.1. PSU prevalence and patterns of use › 3.1.2. Meta-analysis results, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: How many of the 16 sources entered each pooled estimate is shown only in Figure 1 (forest plots), an image that was not viewable in this reading.

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity was extreme in all four pooled analyses: I² 97% to 99%, chi-square p<0.01; random-effects models were used for that reason.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results › 3.1.2. Meta-analysis results, 1st paragraph; 2. Methods › 2.1, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Across sources, co-use among people who use cocaine varied widely: simultaneous alcohol use 24% to 98%, simultaneous cannabis use 12% to 76%, concurrent alcohol use 37% to 96%, concurrent cannabis use 43% to 94% (ranges as stated in the text).
key_findings.locator: 3. Results › 3.1.1. Review of studies including PSU prevalence, 1st paragraph; Table 1, Polysubstance use rate column (note)
key_findings.note: Three of the four ranges do not match Table 1, whose values run 23.5% to 87% (simultaneous alcohol), 9.3% to 76.5% (simultaneous cannabis) and 34.9% to 96.5% (concurrent alcohol); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Definitions differed between sources: simultaneous use meant use at the same time or within a couple of hours, co-administration in a session, co-use at first cocaine use, using alcohol or cannabis to come down from a cocaine high, or using them together with cocaine and a prescription drug in the past 12 months (Rx study); concurrent use meant both substances within 30 days, 6 months, a year or a lifetime, both positive in one urine test, or an unstated window (one source). The review's own definitions were use on the same occasion with overlapping consumption or effects (simultaneous) and use within a specified period (concurrent). Only one source (Grant & Harford, 1990) reported both simultaneous and concurrent use, and several rates had to be calculated by the authors from the articles' data.
key_findings.locator: 3.1.1, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, Measure column; 4. Discussion, 1st paragraph; 2. Methods › 2.1, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The definition changed the figure within the same samples: in the two women-only St Louis samples, using alcohol to come down from a cocaine high in the past 30 days was reported by 23.5% (WTW, n=463) and 36.1% (STOP, n=122) of people who had used cocaine in the past 30 days, cannabis for that purpose by 9.3% and 12.3%, while past-30-day use of alcohol at all was 79.5% and 71.3%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows 13 (Women Teaching Women) and 14 (Sisters Teaching Options for Prevention)

key_findings.finding: The 16 sources: 11 from a single PubMed search (770 records screened, 134 full texts, 11 included; humans, January 1990 to June 2017) and 5 from the authors' secondary analyses (2014 NSDUH, WTW, STOP, Rx, HealthStreet); 10 from the US, 3 Canada, 2 Brazil, 1 Denmark; study periods 1985 to 2017; all but one measured co-use by self-report, one by urine results in emergency-department records.

Treatment data from Tennessee (Kedia et al., 2007, as cited): 48.7% of 36,425 people treated for substance use disorder in 1998–2004 reported polysubstance use; of those reporting cocaine use, 77.8% (n=21,970) did; cocaine with alcohol was the most common two-drug combination (12% of all clients) and cocaine, alcohol and cannabis the most common three-drug combination (8.9%); nicotine was not recorded.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figure. The n of 21,970 can only be the number reporting cocaine use: if it were the number among them who used several substances it would exceed the 48.7% of 36,425 (about 17,700) who reported polysubstance use in the whole sample (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Of the 40 most recent human cocaine neuroimaging studies (to 1 January 2018), none excluded people who drink alcohol or use cannabis (two excluded cannabis use in the past week), 10 excluded alcohol dependence and 10 cannabis dependence; of 40 recent animal cocaine studies, 2 also gave alcohol (both developmental or adolescent-exposure designs) and none cannabis. Co-use was present or modelled in 75% vs 5% (alcohol) and 72.5% vs 0% (cannabis) of human vs animal studies; Fisher's exact test p<0.0001 for both. In most of the human studies, alcohol or cannabis dependence was a reason to exclude the comparison (control) participants, so the cocaine groups and their controls could differ in alcohol and cannabis dependence as well as in cocaine use. The authors add that excluding polysubstance use is valid for some animal questions; their point is that it is rarely considered.
key_findings.locator: 3.3. Exploratory analysis of the frequency of PSU in human and preclinical studies, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: 72.5% implies 29 of 40 human studies, while Table 2 lists 30 that did not exclude cannabis dependence; one of them (Mitchell et al., 2013) sampled no one with cannabis dependence, which may explain the difference. The human and animal percentages measure different things (see interpretation gap).

key_findings.finding: Studies of combined intake are scarce: of more than 3,000 PubMed records for cocaine AND self-administration, fewer than 20 involved simultaneous or concurrent intake of a second substance (authors' count).

As cited from single small human laboratory studies: alcohol taken with cocaine raised plasma cocaine and produced cocaethylene, an active metabolite formed only when alcohol is present (McCance-Katz et al., 1998; Pan & Hedaya, 1999 in rodents); smoked THC before intranasal cocaine raised plasma cocaine (Lukas et al., 1994; men only, according to the cited paper's title in the reference list). The neurobiological effects of taking cocaethylene over long periods have not been assessed, as the review notes.
key_findings.note: Second-hand and unappraised; reported here only as pointers to the primary studies.

key_findings.finding: Monkey studies of alcohol given before cocaine self-administration, as cited, were mixed: no change on average with an increase in 2 of 4 monkeys after one alcohol dose (Aspen & Winger, 1997), in which alcohol also increased self-administration of the dopamine reuptake inhibitor nomifensine; and reduced cocaine intake after the highest alcohol dose with no effect of lower doses (Czoty, 2015). In another phase of the Czoty study, with daily access to sweetened alcohol starting 4 hours after the cocaine sessions, 5 of 6 monkeys self-administered cocaine doses that had not been reinforcing before, and stopped taking those lower doses when the alcohol access ended. These are the findings behind the review's statement that combined cocaine and alcohol increases the reinforcing qualities of dopamine agonists.

As cited from one research group's cross-sectional MRI and MR spectroscopy studies (San Francisco, community and treatment samples): people dependent on both cocaine and alcohol showed more frontal white-matter abnormality and less prefrontal white matter than people with either disorder alone, and in later studies people with alcohol use disorder plus dependence on another drug (76% and 75% of them on cocaine, as described) had a thinner anterior cingulate cortex and some metabolite differences compared with people with alcohol use disorder alone, while other differences (orbitofrontal volume, GABA) were similar; in one study, 17 people with polysubstance use disorders retested after 4 months of abstinence had improved on the measures where they scored worse at baseline.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.3. Neurocognitive correlates of cocaine PSU, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the review states this as a causal effect of combined dependence, which cross-sectional comparisons cannot show.

key_findings.finding: As cited for treatment: in a placebo-controlled trial modafinil reduced cocaine use only in patients without comorbid alcohol use disorder (Anderson et al., 2009); studies of alcohol or cannabis co-use and cocaine treatment outcomes disagree (for example no effect of cannabis use in 186 patients, Budney et al., 1996; shorter time to first cocaine use and no stable remission with cannabis use in 250 patients after inpatient treatment, Aharonovich et al., 2005).
key_findings.locator: 3.2.4. Cocaine PSU and treatment efficacy, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors note that tobacco combined with other substances, particularly alcohol, may be even more frequent than cocaine with alcohol but is not consistently recorded in studies of illicit drug use, and call for data on the timing of co-use and for animal models that reflect it.

reporting_issues.issue: Three of the four ranges stated in the text do not match Table 1: the text gives simultaneous alcohol use 24–98% (Table 1's highest simultaneous alcohol value is 87%, Licht et al., 2012; 98.3% appears only as lifetime concurrent use in the Rx study), simultaneous cannabis use 12–76% (Table 1 shows 9.3% for WTW) and concurrent alcohol use 37–96% (Table 1 shows 34.9% for Vanek et al., 1996).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which values entered each pooled estimate; Figure 1, which would show them, was not viewable (blank screenshots for the first reader, the second reader and the adjudicator). An editors' recalculation from Table 1 under the review's rules (shorter window, powder over crack; DerSimonian–Laird random effects on the logit scale) reproduces two of the four averages exactly, simultaneous cannabis 37.9% (19.7–60.3%) from 7 sources and concurrent alcohol 77.0% (62.1–87.2%) from 11, but gives 70.1% (46.1–86.5%) for simultaneous alcohol (8 sources) and 66.5% (49.5–80.1%) for concurrent cannabis (8 sources), against the printed 74% and 64%, so the inputs to those two cannot be identified (using HealthStreet's alcohol-and-cannabis figure, 43.7%, in place of its cannabis figure gives 64.5%, 47.0–78.8%: possible, unconfirmed).

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name Kedia et al. (2007) among the four clinical samples included, but Table 1 has no Kedia row and lists three clinical or emergency-department samples (Lindsay, Guindalini, Vanek); Table 1 gives the 2005 NSDUH source (Hedden et al., 2009) n=36,425, the figure the Introduction gives for Kedia's Tennessee treatment sample.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): 1. Introduction, 2nd paragraph; 2.1, 3rd paragraph; Table 1, rows 6 and 9–11
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a source is missing from the table or a sample size was transposed between sources; the paper does not allow this to be resolved.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say two studies used the NSDUH but cite three papers (Grant & Harford, 1990; Hedden et al., 2009; Hedden et al., 2010); Hedden et al. (2010) does not appear in Table 1, and the Results count three NSDUH sources, including the authors' own 2014 analysis.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): 2.1, 3rd paragraph; 3.1.1, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but with the previous issue it leaves the list of pooled sources uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The neuroimaging count was to include studies whose outcome was a brain imaging or fMRI measure, but Table 2 includes a cardiac MR spectroscopy study of myocardial steatosis (Lai et al., 2015).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the selection rule was not applied strictly, which does not change the conclusion that few human studies excluded people who drink or use cannabis.
